title: JSON Web Key (JWK)
summary: A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JSON data structure that represents a cryptographic key. The specification also defines a JWK Set, a structure that represents a set of JWKs. Algorithms and identifiers are described in the JSON Web Algorithms specification.

eli5.summary: A JWK is a way of writing down a secret code key as a tidy list. A JWK Set is a ring of such keys.

questions: what does kty mean in a jwk
how do you encrypt a jwk
subtitle: A standard way to write a cryptographic key, or a whole set of keys, as plain JSON.

tldr.problem: Software that signs or encrypts JSON data needs a common, compact way to describe the keys it uses, instead of each system inventing its own format.
tldr.mechanism: A JWK is a JSON object whose members describe one key: its type (kty), its key-specific values, and optional hints such as intended use, algorithm and key ID. A JWK Set is a JSON object with a keys array of JWKs.
tldr.outcome: JWKs and JWK Sets are used by the JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Encryption specifications, and they can themselves be encrypted as a JWE to protect private keys.

today: RFC 7517 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is part of the JOSE family alongside RFC 7515, RFC 7516 and RFC 7518.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A JSON Web Key (JWK) is a JSON data structure that represents a cryptographic key. A JWK Set is a JSON data structure that represents a set of JWKs. The algorithms and identifiers that go with these keys are defined in the separate JSON Web Algorithms (JWA) specification and its IANA registries.

JWKs and JWK Sets are used in the JSON Web Signature (JWS, RFC 7515) and JSON Web Encryption (JWE, RFC 7516) specifications. Names defined by the RFC are deliberately short, because a core goal is compact representations. It is not a goal to represent new kinds of certificate chains or certified keys, or to replace X.509 certificates.
sections.eli5: When programs share a secret-code key they need to write it down the same way. This memo is the agreed way to write it, using short names so it stays small.

sections.title: An Example Key
sections.content:
The RFC's first example is an Elliptic Curve key on the P-256 curve. Its x and y coordinates are base64url-encoded, and a kid (key ID) is included. Appendix A has further examples: public keys, private keys and symmetric keys, for both EC and RSA.

In the RSA examples, integers are represented using the base64url encoding of their big-endian representations.
sections.eli5: A key written as a JWK looks like a small form with boxes: what kind of key, its secret numbers, and a name tag so you can find it later.

sections.title: The JWK Format
sections.content:
A JWK is a JSON object. Its members are the key's properties, including its value. This RFC defines the common parameters that are not algorithm specific. Each JWK also carries members specific to its key type, defined in section 6 of JWA.

Member names within a JWK MUST be unique. Parsers MUST either reject JWKs with duplicate names or use a JSON parser that keeps only the lexically last duplicate. Members a parser does not understand MUST be ignored. New member names should be registered in the IANA JSON Web Key Parameters registry or contain a Collision-Resistant Name.

A JWK Set is a JSON object that MUST have a keys member holding an array of JWKs. The same rules apply for duplicate and unknown members. Implementations SHOULD ignore JWKs in a set whose kty they do not understand, that lack required members, or whose values are out of the supported ranges. Order in the array does not imply preference unless an application gives it that meaning.
sections.eli5: A key card is a list of labelled facts, and each label may appear only once. If a card has a label you do not know, you just skip it. A key ring is a list of such cards.

sections.title: The Common Parameters
sections.content:
kty (key type) names the algorithm family, such as RSA or EC. It is case sensitive and MUST be present in every JWK. The other common parameters are optional.

  • use says whether a public key is for signature (sig) or encryption (enc).
  • key_ops is an array of allowed operations such as sign, verify, encrypt and decrypt. Duplicates MUST NOT appear, and unrelated operations SHOULD NOT be combined for one key.
  • alg names the algorithm intended for the key.
  • kid is used to match a specific key, for instance to pick among keys in a set during key rollover. Different keys in one set SHOULD use distinct kid values.

use and key_ops SHOULD NOT be used together, and if both are present they MUST be consistent.
sections.eli5: On the key card, one box says what kind of key it is, and that box is mandatory. Other boxes say what the key may do and give it a name tag.

sections.title: Linking Keys to X.509 Certificates
sections.content:
Four optional parameters tie a JWK to an X.509 certificate. x5u is a URI pointing to a PEM-encoded certificate or chain; fetching it MUST use integrity protection, and an HTTP GET MUST use TLS with the server identity validated. x5c is an array of base64-encoded (not base64url) DER certificates, with the certificate holding the key first. x5t and x5t#S256 are base64url-encoded SHA-1 and SHA-256 thumbprints of a certificate.

In every case the key in the certificate MUST match the public key given by the other JWK members. If members such as use or alg are also present, they MUST be semantically consistent with the certificate.
sections.eli5: A key card can point at an official ID document that vouches for the key. If it does, the card and the document must agree with each other.

sections.title: Encrypted JWKs
sections.content:
Parties without legitimate access MUST be prevented from reading JWKs that hold private or symmetric key material. The recommended way is an Encrypted JWK: a JWE whose plaintext is the UTF-8 encoding of the JWK. An Encrypted JWK Set works the same way. Processing is identical to any other JWE.

The JWE cty header parameter MUST be jwk+json (or jwk-set+json for a set), unless the application knows the content by other means. Appendix C walks through an encrypted RSA private key.
sections.eli5: If a key card holds a secret, you lock the card in a box. The box carries a note saying a key card is inside.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC creates IANA registries for JWK parameters, JWK use values, JWK key operations values and JWK Set parameters. Registration is Specification Required, after a three-week review on a mailing list, advised by Designated Experts. It also registers the media types application/jwk+json and application/jwk-set+json.

Parameter names SHOULD be short, not exceeding 8 characters without a compelling reason, to keep representations compact.
sections.eli5: There is an official notebook where new box labels get written down, so nobody uses the same label for two different things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Everything pertinent to any cryptographic application applies, including protecting private and symmetric keys. Trust in data secured by a key is no greater than trust in how the key was obtained. Applications usually decide based on attributes bound to a key, for example through a PKIX certificate in x5c, or a JWT claim that carries the JWK or a TLS-secured URI for it.

Private and symmetric keys MUST be protected from disclosure, and encrypting them as a JWE is the recommended way. For RSA, key blinding needs all of n, e and d, so private key representations that omit e should be avoided. Key entropy guidance is deferred to the JWS specification.
sections.eli5: A key is only as trustworthy as the person who handed it to you, and secret keys must never be left lying around.

}
